summary.text: Matrix multiplication turns two matrices into a new matrix, and it works only when the first has as many columns as the second has rows.
Each entry of the product is the dot product of a row of the first matrix with a column of the second.
Binet first described it in 1812 to represent the composition of linear maps, and the order of the factors matters because it is non-commutative.

facts.label: Shape of the product
facts.value: Rows of the first matrix, columns of the second

facts.label: Each entry
facts.value: A row of the first dotted with a column of the second

facts.label: Order matters
facts.value: It is non-commutative, even when both orders are defined

facts.label: Where it is used
facts.value: Statistics, physics, economics, engineering and more

items.prompt: Matrix A has 2 rows and 3 columns, and matrix B has 3 rows and 4 columns. What shape is the product AB?

options.label: 3 rows and 3 columns
4 rows and 2 columns
2 rows and 4 columns
It cannot be formed at all

items.explain: The columns of A match the rows of B, so the product exists, with the rows of the first matrix and the columns of the second.

items.prompt: The first matrix has more columns than the second matrix has rows. Can the two be multiplied in that order?

options.label: No, the columns of the first must equal the rows of the second
Yes, the extra columns are simply ignored
Yes, but only if both matrices are square
No, because the first matrix must be square

items.explain: The product is defined if and only if the number of columns in the first matrix equals the number of rows in the second.

items.prompt: To fill one cell of a product matrix, you pair one row of the first matrix with one column of the second. What do you do with the pair?

options.label: Add matching entries, then multiply the sums
Multiply all the entries together
Pick the larger entry from each pair
Multiply matching entries and add the results

items.explain: The entry is obtained by multiplying term by term the entries of the row and the column and summing those products, which is a dot product.

items.prompt: A friend says that for matrices A and B, AB always equals BA, just like 3 times 5 equals 5 times 3. What is the best reply?

options.label: Correct, matrix multiplication always commutes
No, the order matters even when both products exist
Correct, but only when the matrices are square
No, BA is never defined when AB is

items.explain: Matrix multiplication is non-commutative, even when the product remains defined after changing the order of the factors.

items.prompt: A robot arm turns a point using one matrix, then turns the result again using a second matrix. What does multiplying the two matrices give?

options.label: The average of the two movements
Only the second movement, undone
One matrix for both movements in a row
The difference between the movements

items.explain: Matrix multiplication represents the composition of linear maps, so the product stands for applying one map and then the other.

items.prompt: A row of numbers is multiplied by a column of numbers of the same length. What kind of result do you get?

options.label: A single number, the dot product
Another row of numbers
A square table of numbers
A column of the same length

items.explain: A row times a column gives a 1 × 1 matrix, whose single entry is the dot product. A column times a row gives an n × n matrix instead.
